source.title: Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use to a Single Crosscoder Feature
source.authors: A. Shportko; Shubham Bhokare; Ahmed Zeyad A Alzahrani; Bowen Cheng; Gustavo Mercier; Jessica Hullman

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present, including appendices. Some equations and tables have minor extraction or flattening artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse crosscoders, reconstruction, feature interpretation, and feature steering on an LLM pair to test whether dictionary features capture behaviorally relevant structure. This is a different method and setting from the toy-model claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports feature-level interventions, sparse-dictionary reconstruction outcomes, and decoder-geometry comparisons. Hyperparameter values used only to select steering settings are not recorded as results. The paper's individual sweep outcomes in Table 8 are not reproduced here; the aggregate sweep results are recorded instead.
record.test_reason: The study uses sparse crosscoders (DFC and CrossCoder) as a model-diffing tool on a Qwen2.5-3B RL/base pair. It reports that tool's performance: reconstruction effects on tool correctness, decoder geometry of its own partitions, and steering gains. It cites the superposition hypothesis only as background. None of its results measure whether the model stores more features than dimensions, whether neurons are polysemantic for capacity reasons, or whether dictionary features are canonical or one-dimensional. Autointerp scores cover 10 features pre-selected by Cohen's d; they validate the method's chosen features rather than test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that DFC partitioning concentrates RL-introduced tool-use capability into a minimal steerable feature set: one A-exclusive feature gives +65 pp, generalizing to 7 of 9 layers. They also find the exclusive partition is a filter, not a sink, because joint training delocalizes capability into shared weights and causes spillover to the base model. They interpret this as superposition crossing model boundaries when capabilities are not orthogonal.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses sparse crosscoders and Dedicated Feature Crosscoders, reconstruction, decoder-geometry analysis, automated feature interpretation, and steering on an RL-fine-tuned LLM pair. It does not reproduce the original toy-network method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with architecture (DFC versus CrossCoder), exclusive-partition penalty and share, top-k sparsity, steering partition, feature budget |S|, steering coefficient alpha, and probed layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient-masked DFC partitions form separated decoder regions (k-NN purity 0.984, ARI 0.93). A matched CrossCoder mass-ratio proxy does not (0.158, ARI 0.08, silhouette -0.168).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Partition masks in dedicated-feature crosscoders, not decoder mass asymmetry, produce geometrically separated model-exclusive feature regions.

fits_no_version.finding: Joint crosscoder reconstruction raises the frozen base model's tool correctness from 0% to 6.8% but never its format accuracy. The authors call this evidence that superposition crosses model boundaries.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In joint sparse decompositions of two models, non-orthogonal capability directions are shared across models, enabling capability spillover.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering a single DFC A-exclusive feature gives +65 pp tool correctness, while CrossCoder needs 33 features to reach +70 pp. Combining A-exclusive and shared features interferes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL-induced behaviours can be localized to and steered through very few crosscoder features.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, 2026
record.problems: The study covers one model pair and one task. The architecture comparison uses 12 CrossCoder runs versus 36 DFC runs and is described as underpowered. Steering uses 40 prompts per cell; the best-cell results were not replicated on a fresh sample. Autointerpretation covers only A-exclusive features. The text cautions that Cohen’s d values above approximately 5 reflect near-zero variance under general text and should be read as clean separation rather than comparable effect sizes.
record.rows_left_out: Table 8 reports individual post-reconstruction outcomes for all 48 sweep variants. Those per-variant values are omitted here in favor of the paper's aggregate results in Table 2; the table-level results are not claimed to be identical across variants.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep or geometry of superposed features.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity/importance analysis.
No test of non-capacity sources of polysemanticity.

Does not measure whether features are distributed across neurons or whether sparse features are recovered beyond the method's own selected, steerable features. Autointerp covers only 10 d-ranked A-exclusive features.
No completeness, stability or canonicity tests across seeds, sizes or methods. The 48-variant sweep reports only behavioural reconstruction outcomes.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Penalizing the exclusive partition (lambda_excl = 1e-3) lowers Model A delta (34.8 to 25.8 pp at 5% share; 35.2 to 32.0 pp at 10% share). This is the 'filter, not sink' result.
Training MSE correlates only weakly with Model A gain (r = +0.08, CI [-0.21, +0.36]).

record.verdict_notes: This is a model-diffing and steering paper. Superposition appears only as motivation and in a discussion remark. All reader links to V4 are removed and no verdicts are given. The reader's V4 'supports' label rested on steering efficacy and autointerp of d-selected features, which is own-method performance (T4). Only 4 of the 10 listed features meet the paper's 0.8 detection threshold.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular superposition geometry.
Does not test polysemantic neurons or whether feature importance and capacity competition cause some features to receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemanticity can arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
Tests sparse crosscoder features in one Qwen2.5-3B model pair on ToolRL tool use; does not test other LLMs, tasks, or SAE methods generally.
Does not establish whether SAE or crosscoder features are complete, stable, or canonical units across methods, models, or settings.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features as alternative units of superposition.

rows.note: The authors call this capability spillover and report that it occurs without fine-tuning.
